The hybrid approach delivers actionable improvement immediately while building organizational capability incrementally, and the targeted scope creates a manageable learning environment for the accounting staff that serves as a natural precursor to broader ABC adoption if justified by future complexity growth.
SourceDescription: Original CMA Part 1 content by AI-assisted authoring under Framework v2.
ExplanationWrongA: Full ABC implementation provides the most complete and accurate product-cost information, and the argument that strategic mispricing risk justifies the investment is well-founded. If the specialty flexible heater line is indeed priced 24 percentage points below its true cost (from +18% apparent margin to -6% actual margin), every dollar of revenue in this segment destroys shareholder value, and the $525,000 implementation cost is small relative to the cumulative losses that would accrue over the years the company continues mispricing its fastest-growing product family. The limitation is one of organizational readiness and cost-benefit proportionality. Implementing a full five-pool ABC system requires not just the initial $340,000 technology investment but an ongoing annual commitment of $185,000 for data maintenance that creates a permanent fixed cost increase. If the accounting staff lacks ABC expertise, the system may produce unreliable data that is worse than the plantwide method--inaccurately precise rather than approximately accurate. Moreover, applying ABC to the standard cartridge heater line (72% of volume) delivers minimal decision-improvement benefit because these products are commodities whose prices are set by the market, not by cost-plus formulas. The incremental accuracy is genuine but the incremental decision value is near zero for the majority of the company's volume.
ExplanationWrongC: A material-cost-based surcharge represents a pragmatic, low-cost response to the cost-distortion problem: it recognizes that complexity drives overhead consumption and that material cost can serve as a proxy for complexity in many manufacturing environments, where complex products tend to use more expensive or more varied materials. The approach requires no new data-collection systems, no staff training, and can be implemented within a single accounting period at negligible cost. The limitation is that material cost is a weak proxy for the specific overhead drivers that actually cause the cost distortion. The specialty flexible heater line may use relatively inexpensive materials (flexible polymer substrates) while consuming disproportionate quantities of engineering support (for custom designs) and machine setups (for small production batches). A material-cost surcharge would systematically undercost products with low material cost but high complexity and overcost products with high material cost but low complexity, which is precisely the opposite of the correction needed. Moreover, the surcharge approach lacks the activity-level transparency that allows managers to understand and manage the drivers of overhead cost--it buries the complexity cost in an arbitrary markup rather than revealing it as a manageable activity that could potentially be reduced through process improvement.
ExplanationWrongD: Deferring ABC implementation while investing in staff training addresses the capability constraint that is the most frequently cited reason for ABC implementation failures. Organizations that adopt ABC without adequate training typically produce unreliable cost data, lose confidence in the system, and revert to simpler methods within two to three years. An 18-month training period allows the accounting team to develop genuine expertise, pilot the methodology on a limited scale, and build organizational buy-in before committing to a full implementation. The time-driven ABC variant further reduces ongoing costs by using time equations (estimated process times for each activity) rather than transactional activity drivers that require extensive data collection. The limitation is the cost of delay: the specialty flexible heater line is losing money on every unit sold today, and an 18-month deferral means 18 additional months of value destruction in what the CEO has identified as the company's strategic growth segment. Additionally, customer relationships and pricing expectations are being built on a cost structure that the company knows is wrong; the longer the mispricing continues, the harder it will be to raise prices to economically sustainable levels without damaging customer relationships. The capability-building objective is legitimate, but it should be pursued in parallel with a targeted intervention, not as a substitute for immediate corrective action on the most severely distorted product costs.

Topic: D.E05 pricing strategy selection with competitive, cost, and customer value constraints
MicroTopic: evaluating cost-plus, target costing, market-based, and value-based pricing approaches
Stem: NovaScan Medical has developed a portable diagnostic imaging device that performs three common radiology scans at the point of care. The device's manufacturing cost is $18,400 per unit at projected volumes of 1,200 units annually, with a cost structure of direct materials ($7,200), direct labor ($4,100), variable overhead ($2,800), and allocated fixed overhead ($4,300). The company's traditional cost-plus pricing formula applies a 40% markup on full manufacturing cost, yielding a target price of $25,760. Market research indicates that competing stationary imaging systems--which are less portable but functionally equivalent--sell for $22,000 to $32,000 depending on configuration. Customer willingness-to-pay surveys of hospital procurement officers suggest a value-based price range of $24,500 to $29,500 based on estimated workflow savings of $35,000 to $50,000 annually per device from reduced patient transfer time, faster diagnosis, and improved emergency department throughput. NovaScan's primary competitor, established in stationary imaging, has announced a competing portable device at an expected price of $22,900, launching in 14 months. NovaScan's investors expect a 25% gross margin on revenue, and the company's five-year strategy requires building an installed base of at least 800 units within 24 months to create switching costs that protect against the competitor's entry. The VP of Marketing advocates penetration pricing at $21,500 to maximize installed base; the CFO advocates cost-plus at $25,760 to ensure margin targets; the VP of Sales advocates value-based pricing at $27,900 to capture a share of the documented workflow savings. Which pricing strategy should the CEO adopt?

Choices.A: Cost-plus pricing at $25,760 (full manufacturing cost plus 40% markup) because it guarantees the 25% gross margin target, provides a clear and defensible pricing rationale, and positions the product within the competitive range established by stationary imaging systems
Choices.B: Market-based pricing at $22,500 to undercut the announced competitor by a modest margin, signal price competitiveness to early adopter hospitals, and accelerate installed-base growth toward the 800-unit strategic target while still earning a positive contribution margin
Choices.C: Target costing approach: set the price at the customer willingness-to-pay midpoint of $27,000, work backward to identify $4,800 in per-unit cost reductions through design simplification, supplier negotiation, and volume efficiencies, and capture margin while the product enjoys a 14-month window of limited competition
Choices.D: Value-based pricing at $27,900 with a performance-guarantee program that protects hospitals against productivity shortfalls, justifying the premium through documented workflow savings of $35,000 to $50,000 annually per device that make the device's price a fraction of the value delivered

ExplanationCorrect: The target costing approach is the recommended strategy because it directly addresses the unique temporal dynamics of NovaScan's competitive situation: a 14-month window of limited competition followed by the entry of a well-established rival at an aggressive price point. Target costing begins with the market-determined price and works backward to achieve the required margin through cost reduction, rather than beginning with cost and marking up to a price the market may not support. Setting the initial price at $27,000--the midpoint of the customer willingness-to-pay range--positions the product at a premium that reflects its differentiation (portability, point-of-care capability, documented workflow savings) without testing the upper bound of what procurement officers will accept. This price is above the competitor's announced $22,900, which is appropriate during the 14-month exclusivity window when NovaScan's portability advantage is unique. The $4,800 per-unit cost reduction target is ambitious but structurally achievable: at projected volumes of 1,200 units, direct materials ($7,200) may yield 8-12% savings through volume-based supplier negotiation and component standardization; direct labor ($4,100) can benefit from learning-curve effects as production experience accumulates; and variable overhead ($2,800) typically includes items amenable to process improvement. The cost-plus approach (Option A) at $25,760 guarantees the margin mathematically but ignores the fundamental pricing principle that costs determine whether a price is acceptable, not what the price should be. If the competitor enters at $22,900 and NovaScan is priced at $25,760, the company will struggle to achieve the 800-unit installed base target as price-sensitive hospitals defer purchasing decisions or negotiate aggressively. Market-based pricing at $22,500 (Option B) would likely accelerate installed-base growth but at the expense of leaving substantial value on the table during the 14-month monopoly window--hospitals are willing to pay $24,500 to $29,500, and pricing near the bottom of that range sacrifices margin that could fund the R&D pipeline for the next-generation device. Value-based pricing at $27,900 (Option D) appropriately quantifies the customer's economic benefit but at the top of the willingness-to-pay range, it risks slow adoption that fails to build the installed base before the competitor enters. When the competitor launches at $22,900, hospitals that paid $27,900 may feel buyer's remorse, and those still evaluating will have a powerful reason to wait. The target costing approach at $27,000 with a commitment to cost reduction balances premium positioning, margin capture, and adoption velocity while building the organizational discipline to compete on cost when the market inevitably becomes more price-competitive after competitor entry. This strategy also creates optionality: if the cost-reduction program succeeds, NovaScan can maintain margin as competitive pressure intensifies; if it partially succeeds, the company has built a customer base and can adjust pricing from a position of installed-base strength.

ExplanationWrongA: Cost-plus pricing at $25,760 has genuine strengths that should not be dismissed: it mathematically guarantees the 25% gross margin that investors require ($25,760 minus $18,400 equals $7,360, or 28.6% of revenue), and it provides a consistent, defensible pricing methodology that the board and investors can understand and monitor. For a company with a single product in its early commercialization phase, cost-plus eliminates pricing uncertainty and ensures that every unit sold contributes to fixed-cost recovery and profit. The limitation is that cost-plus pricing is internally focused--it answers the question of what price the company needs to achieve its financial targets, not what price the market will support. The $25,760 figure falls within the competitive range but near the middle; when the competitor enters at $22,900 in 14 months, NovaScan will face a price gap of nearly $3,000 per unit against an established rival with existing hospital relationships. The 25% margin target is being achieved on paper but may not be achievable in the market if volume falls short because the price is uncompetitive. Cost-plus also provides no incentive for cost reduction--if anything, it rewards cost inflation by mechanically increasing the price--and fails to capture the value created for customers, leaving money on the table that could fund growth or reward investors.
ExplanationWrongB: Market-based pricing at $22,500 is strategically coherent with the installed-base objective: by pricing below the announced competitor ($22,900) and well below the customer willingness-to-pay range, NovaScan maximizes early adoption velocity and builds the switching-cost protection that the five-year strategy requires. The $4,100 contribution margin per unit ($22,500 minus $18,400) is positive and contributes to fixed-cost coverage, and the volume acceleration may more than compensate for the lower per-unit margin through operating leverage as fixed costs are spread over more units. The limitation is that this strategy cedes approximately $4,500 to $5,400 per unit in value that hospitals have indicated they are willing to pay, and it permanently anchors the product's price at a discount level before the competitor even enters the market. Once hospitals become accustomed to a $22,500 price point for portable diagnostic imaging, raising prices becomes extremely difficult, and the competitor's $22,900 entry may trigger a price war that neither company wins but the larger, better-capitalized rival can sustain longer. The 800-unit installed-base target is important, but achieving it through price alone sacrifices the margin that funds the innovation cycle needed to maintain the product's differentiation advantage over time. A market-share strategy that destroys industry profitability is typically value-destructive for the innovator who bears the R&D cost.
ExplanationWrongD: Value-based pricing at $27,900 with a performance-guarantee program represents the most sophisticated pricing approach: it quantifies the customer's economic benefit ($35,000 to $50,000 in annual workflow savings), positions the device's price as a small fraction of the value delivered, and uses a guarantee mechanism to overcome the adoption barrier that hospital procurement officers face when evaluating new medical technology from an unproven vendor. This approach can command premium margins during the period when NovaScan's portability advantage is unique and unduplicated. The limitation is adoption velocity risk. At $27,900, NovaScan is pricing at the upper end of the willingness-to-pay range, and hospitals evaluating a $28,000 capital equipment purchase from a new entrant will conduct extended due diligence, reference checks, and committee reviews before committing. With a 14-month competitor launch window, the sales cycle length at a premium price point may prevent NovaScan from achieving the 800-unit installed base before the competitor enters. When the competitor launches at $22,900, hospitals that have not yet purchased will face a clear choice: a proven competitor's device at a significantly lower price versus NovaScan's device at a premium. The performance guarantee reduces perceived risk but does not eliminate the price-comparison dynamic, and risk-averse hospital procurement committees may default to the lower-priced, established-vendor option regardless of guarantee terms. Value-based pricing maximizes per-unit profitability but may achieve it at volumes too low to create sustainable competitive advantage.
